paras.en: You might even be able to sell some of the energy stored in your car's battery back to the grid. EV owners could charge during the day or late at night, when the demand for electricity is lower and pay lower rates for electricity. Then, in the evenings when the electrical grid is under more strain and the price of electricity is higher, they could sell that stored energy back at a profit.

Standardized software programs that throttle EV charging speeds during peak hours already exist. Drivers can use them if, for example, they want to keep charging costs down by primarily charging their cars during off-peak hours when electricity costs are lower, or if they want to use electricity only from solar power to charge, said Rajit Gadh, a researcher who studies EV charging and scalability at UCLA. But the process for sending energy back to the grid is a different story. Individual manufacturers haven't yet landed on a standard way to tell cars when and how much energy to discharge, Gadh said.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "What is needed is really [for] every EV charging vendor — and every EV manufacturer, actually — to have this protocol built in, adhere to it in its full specification, and make it available," Gadh told Live Science.

With the right protocols, though, cars of the future will be able to do more than interface with the electrical grid. "Vehicle-to-everything" technologies could enable cars to communicate with infrastructure and other vehicles to avoid traffic and collisions.

Some cars today are already equipped with vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications. These systems use short-range radio signals to alert other V2V-equipped vehicles of the car's speed, direction of travel and braking patterns. The radio signals can travel about 1,000 feet (300 meters), allowing the vehicle to receive data from cars that are not in the driver's line of sight.

V2V systems could help reduce traffic collisions by warning drivers about oncoming cars they can't see yet — for example, by alerting a driver to another car speeding toward an intersection or coming around a bend as the driver is passing another vehicle on a twisty, two-lane highway. Not all cars have the technology, though, so its practical utility is limited for now.

Some driver assistance technologies, such as lane departure warnings and cruise control, have been on the market in personal cars for decades. These technologies and more recent assistive features require the driver to be in control of the vehicle, but theoretically, they make driving easier. For example, Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) mode handles most steering and braking tasks, but safe operation requires the driver to keep their eyes on the road and be ready to take over at a moment’s notice. In the next several years, drivers will likely see new features that automate driving in more contexts.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Some of these features will allow drivers to take their attention off the road entirely and enjoy some in-car entertainment, as long as they're alert and able to retake control of the vehicle within a few seconds if conditions change. Technologies that fully automate driving in many circumstances within certain service areas will likely be in about 4% of cars on the market by 2035, according to a white paper from the World Economic Forum.

In cars equipped with these features, "you're still going to have driver controls, but under certain circumstances, it will be effectively an automated vehicle," Luke Neurauter, who leads the Division of Vehicle, Driver and System Safety at the Virginia Tech Transportation Institute, told Live Science.

Mercedes-Benz introduced its Drive Pilot system for two consumer car lines in 2022. On the entire German Autobahn network and on certain freeways between and around Los Angeles, San Francisco and Las Vegas, during heavy traffic, the system lets the driver turn their attention toward other activities, such as reading a book or eating lunch, while the car handles steering and keeping pace with other nearby vehicles.

But as the artificial intelligence (AI) models that control autonomous driving improve and become better able to handle unusual scenarios — often called "edge" or "corner" cases — on the road, drivers will be able to hand over control to their cars in more situations, said Rahul Jain, an electrical and computer engineer at the University of Southern California.

Future AI systems might "have some reasoning ability, and then because of that, it can handle these corner cases much better than current systems are able to do," Jain told Live Science. For example, a car might be able to better respond to an indecisive pedestrian who suddenly enters a crossing, assess whether to enter potentially hazardous conditions such as flooded roads, or safely navigate around unusual circumstances, such as construction work, on a highway.

While some systems will enable drivers to make fewer decisions, others that may roll out in the next several years will track a driver's attention and alert them with sounds, an indicator light or haptic feedback when their focus falters. These systems use cameras and software to track head position, eye movement and steering-wheel input to ensure drivers are focused on the road even when they're using assistive features such as lane centering, Neurauter said.

In addition to looking for distracted driving, the technology might expand to monitor drivers for fatigue and alcohol impairment, he added. That information could then affect "whether or not other features become active, or change how they act, based on the driver state at that moment in time," Neurauter said. Proposed legislation could make this technology a requirement in new vehicles as early as 2027, but technological hurdles and concerns over privacy and false positives could stall its implementation.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The technology could also assist drivers who become unable to safely operate the vehicle — for example, if the driver falls asleep or experiences a medical emergency. If a car detects that the driver is not holding the steering wheel or actively controlling the vehicle, it could send a series of visible, audible, or tactile alerts. If the driver doesn’t respond to those cues, a car might turn on its hazard lights and come to a stop. Some vehicle manufacturers are already rolling out such technology; for example, Volkswagen has made it available in all new vehicles from model year 2025.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While personal cars may not offer full automation, highly automated car services will become much more common as rideshare vehicles in major metro areas. In some cities, like San Francisco, commuters already rely heavily on autonomous vehicles from Waymo. The company has rolled out its cars in nearly a dozen cities — including Dallas, Houston, Atlanta and Los Angeles — and has announced plans to expand service to more than 20 additional locales. Other companies — such as Nuro and Volkswagen’s MOIA — are testing their vehicles with human drivers on board before rolling out full public service.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Currently, autonomous vehicles navigate by combining information from preloaded, high-resolution maps and real-time radar, lidar and visual data collected by cameras and sensors attached to the car. An onboard computer uses that information to build a 3D map of its surroundings. Right now, the cost of these sensors makes them impractical for consumer vehicles, Jain said, but they’re becoming cheaper as manufacturers scale up production. The cars also use an AI model trained on both common and unusual driving situations to anticipate how other vehicles and pedestrians will behave and plot a safe path forward, Jain added.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Developing those high-resolution maps takes time, which is one of the main reasons autonomous rideshares aren’t available everywhere yet. Mapping usually involves decking out a car with high-end visual sensors and lasers and driving it throughout the region. Although cities like San Francisco have been mapped with this level of precision, much of the U.S. has not.
"It's very difficult to do overnight," said John Dolan, an autonomous-driving researcher at the Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute.

Complexities also tend to arise in city environments, where unexpected stops are more common and there are many pedestrians who behave unpredictably or jaywalk. But interstate highway driving doesn't face as many of those obstacles, and that could enable autonomous long-haul drives.

"[Autonomous] trucking, I would expect, would be the first thing that's going to happen" in terms of autonomous travel outside of major cities, Jain said. A few driverless trucks are already on the road: Pittsburgh-based company Aurora deployed the technology on I-45 in Texas, between Dallas and Houston, in 2025, with plans to expand across the southern U.S.
While there's speculation involved in predicting the range of self-driving capabilities available in a decade, the picture for EVs is a little clearer.

Right now, lithium-ion batteries dominate the EV market. Each cell in a lithium-ion battery has two electrodes, commonly a layered graphite electrode and a metal oxide or phosphate electrode, separated by a liquid electrolyte solution. Lithium ions migrate back and forth between these two electrodes when a person charges and discharges the battery.

Many electric cars with lithium-ion batteries can already travel more than 300 miles (480 km) on a charge. But that's not ideal for a long-range car trip, because charging stations are few and far between in the country's vast interior and charging takes longer than filling up a gas tank.

Solid-state batteries, which replace the liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte made of ceramic, polymer or sulfide materials, could make that cross-country trip in an EV a practical option, allowing an electric car to travel more than 750 miles (1,200 km) on a single charge. Some prototype battery packs can already achieve this range under controlled conditions. If a solid electrolyte were paired with an anode made of pure lithium, rather than graphite or hard carbon, it would allow the battery to store more energy than a lithium-ion cell of similar mass can.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Solid-state batteries may also enable faster charging. In current batteries that use liquid electrolytes, charging and discharging the battery too quickly can cause dendrites, thin branches of lithium that stretch across the cell and short-circuit the battery. A solid electrolyte could, in theory, block those dendrites, which would enable cars to charge fully in just 10 to 15 minutes. The higher energy density from a lithium metal anode also translates to a greater range than that from a similarly sized lithium-ion battery, Eric Wachsman, director of the Maryland Energy Innovation Institute at the University of Maryland, told Live Science.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Many of the raw materials that go into existing lithium-ion batteries are concentrated in a handful of geographic areas. In 2023, Australia, China and Chile mined about 85% of that year's lithium supply; China mined the majority of graphite used that year as well. And battery materials still make up a significant portion of an electric vehicle's cost.

Sodium-ion batteries could be cheaper and easier to source. Sodium is plentiful in Earth's crust, which means mining could be done throughout the U.S., potentially with a comparatively low environmental impact.

Such batteries also rely on a more widely available electrode material. Sodium ions are larger than lithium ions, so they don't fit in between layers of graphite like lithium ions do. Instead, sodium-ion batteries use hard carbon electrodes.

"When you cook at home and your soup boils over and you get this black ring around your pot, this is hard carbon," Maximilian Fichtner, a solid-state chemist at the Helmholtz Institute Ulm for Electrochemical Energy Storage in Germany, told Live Science. "You can produce this from sucrose or from biomass, from whatever. You can do that everywhere."

The downside is that hard carbon holds less sodium than graphite holds lithium, said Eric McCalla, a battery materials chemist at McGill University in Canada. That means sodium-ion batteries can't store as much energy relative to their mass, and they don't last quite as long as their lithium counterparts.
"The range won't be as large," McCalla told Live Science. "It'll be a fantastic commuter car, but you're not going to go on a family trip from Montreal to California so easily."

Manufacturers are already bringing sodium-ion technology to market. For instance, the Chinese company CATL began mass-producing the batteries in February and claims that their battery packs enable EV ranges over 250 miles (400 km).

But new technologies are being developed rapidly. For example, some scientists are making sodium-ion batteries that use solid electrolytes, combining the higher energy density of solid-state lithium batteries with the cost savings of sodium batteries.

This hybrid battery chemistry is still in the early stages of development, experts told Live Science. "I would be surprised to see them in cars in the next decade," McCalla told Live Science in an email. "I've been surprised before, though."
The future we're describing is the utopian scenario. But the biggest obstacles are likely not technological but rather regulatory, economic, political or cultural, experts said.

"We're going to try to guess at a timeline of when some of these things are going to come in, and odds are, we're going to be wrong," McCalla told Live Science. "Odds are, we're going to be slower than we think."

Solar panels may not wind up being the most economic or practical way to increase EVs' range, while scaling up manufacturing capacity for next-generation batteries is expensive and could slow EV adoption in the U.S. The utility of vehicle-to-vehicle communications, meanwhile, could be limited by a slow rollout and adoption of V2V-equipped cars among drivers.

Whether EVs will be ubiquitous will likely come down to their affordability relative to gas-powered vehicles, which is affected not just by manufacturing and technological advances but also domestic policy choices, such as whether to subsidize EVs or their charging networks.

One challenge for manufacturers is that the automated features drivers prefer may not always be safer. A recent review of automated systems found that those focused on driver safety, such as automatic safety or lane centering, tend to reduce crashes, while those focused on comfort, such as adaptive cruise control, can increase accidents. The authors proposed that such systems make it easier for people to disengage or become distracted while driving and possibly overestimate the capabilities of the system.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And there are other kinks to work out for autonomous rideshare vehicles. In December 2025, a horde of Waymos stalled during a power outage, clogging San Francisco intersections. The cars are programmed to treat dark traffic signals as four-way stops, according to a statement from Waymo, but they occasionally ping human operators for confirmation. During the outage, the number of confirmation requests spiked, leading to delayed responses — and lengthy traffic jams. The company says it has since released software updates that allow its vehicles to act more decisively at dark signals. But questions remain about how the fleet will respond in natural disasters, and some have expressed frustration that autonomous rideshare vehicles already slow down ambulances, fire trucks and police cars responding to emergencies.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: One of the biggest roadblocks to automated driving is the regulatory environment, Neurauter said. Regulations on self-driving vehicles vary by state, and some, such as New York, effectively prohibit driverless vehicles entirely. Where they are legal, they often must carry higher insurance and pass testing, which could limit their rollout.

"When we get into automated driving, the driving behavior is being governed by software that's installed on a computer that's in the vehicle," Steven Shladover, a research engineer at the University of California, Berkeley, told Live Science. "That gets us into a messy gray area where both the federal and the state roles kind of overlap, and that's politically very complicated." For example, different states could end up with different rules for establishing who's legally responsible for an accident involving automated driving.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In 10 years, you'll almost certainly be able to drive from Los Angeles to Las Vegas in an autonomous vehicle. But if you want to drive to New York City, you might have to stop in New Jersey — and take a train into the city.

Skyler Ware is a freelance science journalist covering chemistry, biology, paleontology and Earth science. She was a 2023 AAAS Mass Media Science and Engineering Fellow at Science News. Her work has also appeared in Science News Explores, ZME Science and Chembites, among others. Skyler has a Ph.D. in chemistry from Caltech.

articles.title: A Century Ago, an Extinct Crocodilian's Skull Was Found in the Rocks That Built the Sphinx. Turns Out, It Belonged to a New Species

paras.en: Around 4,500 years ago, ancient Egyptians carved the Great Sphinx of Giza out of limestone in the Mokattam rock formation. Little did they know, the material they were digging through preserved something even more archaic: fossils of a long-extinct crocodile.

Researchers have identified a previously unknown species of gavial, a type of crocodilian with a long, thin snout, from a fossil originally found in the rock formation that the ancient Egyptians sculpted into the Sphinx and the Pyramids of Giza. The new identification corrects a previous erroneous classification, according to a study published October 7 in the journal Royal Society Open Science. It also sheds light on the fauna that existed in what’s now Egypt well before human-made monuments appeared on the horizon.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In the 1920s, several fossilized remains, including a largely intact crocodile-like skull, emerged from the roughly 45-million-year-old Mokattam Formation at a site near Cairo. Because of the bones’ resemblance to those of Tomistoma schlegelii—a living gavial native to Indonesia and Malaysia—experts originally assigned them to the same Tomistoma genus. Until now, the well-preserved skull was the holotype, or name-bearing representative fossil, for the extinct T. cairense.

Thanks to modern paleontological techniques like micro-CT scanning, which allows researchers to see inside fossils without breaking them, the team behind the new work found many differences between Tomistoma and the Mokattam Formation crocs. Comparing measurements of the skull to those of modern and fossil gavials revealed that the roughly 18-inch-long noggin represented not just a new species, but a new genus as well.

They named it Herugavialis cairensis, drawing inspiration from the Egyptian god Heru, also known as Horus. Some Egyptian texts call the Sphinx “Horus of the Horizon.” The associations between the H. cairensis skull and the iconic Sphinx go beyond the material that yielded them. Both are missing the tips of their noses.
Did you know? The origin of the Sphinx’s name

The Egyptians did not refer to the great statue as the Sphinx. Rather, ancient Greeks started calling it that around 2,000 years after it was carved. They possibly did so because of its resemblance to their mythological sphinx, which had a lion’s body, a woman’s head and an eagle’s wings.

“We seek to connect Egypt’s deep natural history with its human history and the legacy of ancient Egyptian civilization,” study co-author Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University in Egypt, tells the Washington Post’s Elijah Wolfson. “Crocodiles were part of the Nile ecosystem, which was central to Egyptian life, and they held an important place in ancient Egyptian belief and culture.”

Gavials, cousins of crocodiles and alligators, were once found throughout the world. The Mediterranean region was home to a diverse community of crocodilians, including gavials, during much of the last 50 million years, lead author Paul Burke, a paleontologist at the Swedish Museum of Natural History, says in a statement. In fact, H. cairensis would have shared its shallow marine habitat with at least two other gavial species. Today, however, there are only two surviving gavials: the previously mentioned T. schlegelii and Gavialis gangeticus, which is clinging to habitats in Nepal and northern India.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Both are endangered, Burke tells Science News’ Jake Buehler. “So we should know about them and their long history.”

Correcting the fossil species’ identification also “helps paint a better picture of what large predators were like in the region,” Alex Hastings, a paleontologist at the Science Museum of Minnesota who did not participate in the study, tells CNN’s Taylor Nicioli. “This expands the known variety of forms of these amazing long-snouted crocodilians across the Mediterranean in ancient times.”

articles.title: This One-of-a-Kind Bronze Ring Offers a Tantalizing Glimpse at the Lighthouse of Alexandria, a Lost Wonder of the Ancient World

paras.en: In ancient times, travelers journeying to Egypt via the Mediterranean Sea often faced perilous conditions.

As the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus wrote in the first century B.C.E., a sandbank extended along much of the kingdom’s northern coast, “not discernible to any who approach without previous experience of these waters.” Sailors who “in their ignorance turn with gladness toward the shore suffer unexpected shipwreck when their vessels suddenly run aground,” Diodorus added, “and now and then, mariners who cannot see land in time because the country lies so low are cast ashore before they realize it.” The only “safe harbor” to be found on this stretch of coastline, the historian concluded, was Pharos, the island that housed the Lighthouse of Alexandria.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Standing an estimated 330 to 430 feet tall, the lighthouse was also known as Pharos, after the land where it stood. At the time of its creation in the third century B.C.E., it was one of the world’s tallest humanmade structures, second only to the Pyramids of Giza. The lighthouse dominated the landscape for more than a millennium, until the 14th century C.E., when it crumbled into the sea following a series of earthquakes.

Some 700 years later, few traces of the lighthouse remain. But excavations on the neighboring island of Antirhodos, the site of an ancient palace that hosted the likes of Mark Antony and Cleopatra, have revealed a rare artifact linked to this lost wonder: a bronze signet ring depicting Pharos.

The ring is the “first of its kind known to exist,” the European Institute for Underwater Archaeology (IEASM) notes in a statement. Its design bears resemblance to portrayals of the lighthouse on Egyptian coins from the second century C.E. As archaeologist Isabelle Hairy writes for the Center for Alexandrian Studies, ancient currency offers “the most important documentary evidence” of Pharos’ appearance, suggesting that it had three tiers, including a square base, an octagonal middle section and a circular top. (Ancient writers left behind descriptions of the lighthouse, but these accounts are often conflicting, resulting in varying visual interpretations by later artists.)
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Need to know: Wonders of the ancient world

- The structures most often cited as the seven wonders of the ancient world are the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Colossus of Rhodes, the Lighthouse of Alexandria, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon.
- Of these seven, only the Great Pyramid of Giza survives today.

Researchers from the institute recovered the ring as part of a joint archaeological mission with the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities. According to a Facebook post shared by the ministry, archaeologists at the site have also found tableware, amphorae, oil lamps and fragments of glassware spanning the fourth century B.C.E. through the fourth century C.E.

“The discovery … is even more important, as [the ring] has been excavated in the legendary palace of the island of Antirhodos, that once upon a time was a center of power,” says Franck Goddio, IEASM’s founder and president, in the statement. The Greek geographer Strabo, who visited Alexandria in the first century B.C.E., described Antirhodos as “an isle lying off the artificial harbor, which has both a royal palace and a small harbor.” Its name, he added, was an allusion to its status as “a rival” of the Greek island of Rhodes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For now, much about the ring remains unknown. “The statement does not say who wore this ring or what for,” Guillermo Carvajal writes for La Brújula Verde. “It gives neither its size nor its exact date.”

Still, the jewelry’s presence at the site has led the researchers to posit that the island once housed administrative offices designated for such tasks as management of the lighthouse. In ancient Egypt, bureaucrats used signet rings to sign legal documents; the pricey accessories also advertised their owners’ elite social status.

Construction of the lighthouse probably began during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter, a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who served as Egypt’s first Ptolemaic king, and wrapped up under his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus, who succeeded him upon his death in 282 B.C.E. The Greek architect Sostratus of Cnidos designed the revolutionary structure, which is often described as the world’s first recorded lighthouse.

Today, physical evidence of Pharos is limited largely to stone blocks and metal clamps used to bind these blocks together. “The architectural fragments lie scattered over 18 acres underwater,” Hairy told the New York Times’ Franz Lidz earlier this year. “The visibility is extremely bad, the seabed is uneven and there are no clear layers of sediment.”

These challenges haven’t stopped Hairy and her colleagues at the Pharos Project from embarking on a multidisciplinary effort to reconstruct the ancient wonder digitally, piecing together photogrammetry scans of the lighthouse’s sparse ruins to envision what it might have looked like in its heyday.

Although Hairy estimates that the work is “still generations from completion,” per the Times, the project’s findings are poised to transform historians’ understanding of the fabled lighthouse. Until then, those hoping to see Pharos for themselves need look no further than the newly discovered ring.

articles.title: Scientists Took a Cheek Swab From the World's Oldest Tortoise. His DNA Could Reveal Hints to Longevity

paras.en: Throughout world wars, pandemics and the turn of centuries, there was Jonathan. As the world around him shifted and changed, he lived the slow life munching grass on Saint Helena, a British island territory some 1,200 miles off the western coast of Africa.

The Aldabra giant tortoise is the oldest turtle in recorded history and the world’s oldest living land animal. Caretakers don’t know his exact age, but a photograph from 1882 shows the tortoise looking fully grown, which, for his species, is at least 50 years old. This means that Jonathan would be about 194 today.
“To be honest, I suspect he’s older,” veterinarian Joe Hollins, who looks after Jonathan, told the Washington Post’s Cathy Free in 2022. “But we can never know.”

No matter Jonathan’s exact age, one thing seems certain: Something has made him exceptional when it comes to withstanding the test of time. He has already lived more than a century beyond his species’ 80-year average life expectancy—a feat that his safe environment, diet and medical care alone might not be able to explain.

In a new study published on Wednesday in Science Advances, researchers examined Jonathan’s DNA for genetic clues to his extraordinary age. To collect the data, Hollins propped Jonathan’s mouth open with a gloved finger and swabbed a sample of cheek cells and saliva.

“We almost never get to study an animal this old while it is still alive,” says co-author Steve Horvath, a biologist who studies aging at the University of California, Los Angeles, to the New York Times’ Monique Brouillette.
Key context: False reports of Jonathan’s death

In April, false reports that Jonathan had died were circulated widely, stemming from a fake X post claiming to be the tortoise’s veterinarian. It turned out to be a hoax—a ploy for cryptocurrency donations.

The research team sequenced Jonathan’s DNA and identified 287 genetic variants that were unique to him. Many of these had to do with repairing damage to DNA, reducing inflammation and managing insulin. They also found that he shared aging-related genes with species including naked mole-rats, which almost never get cancer.

Additionally, they looked at Jonathan’s epigenome, the chemical tags on DNA that turn certain genes on and off. As organisms age, these switches become less predictable—tags might inconsistently attach or fall off, leading to erratic activity from genes. The team compared Jonathan’s epigenome with those of four younger tortoises.

Overall, Jonathan showed the chaos, or entropy, in the epigenome that would be expected for his age. But in the areas of the genome linked to things like DNA repair and mitochondria, the energy-producing centers in cells, Jonathan’s chemical tags were especially youthful. At these spots, Jonathan’s epigenome looked similar to DNA from a 5-year-old juvenile tortoise that the researchers studied.

The work doesn’t prove that these markers are the reason for Jonathan’s long life, but they offer a clue to how DNA might endure for long periods. They also align with findings from supercentenarians, humans who have lived to be more than 110 years old.

“Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face,” study co-author Stephen Clark, founder and chief scientist at the nonprofit Kallel Foundation for aging research, says in a statement. “Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people.”

But before any of this information can find a medical use, scientists will have to conduct deeper research. For one, Jonathan’s cheek swab contained incomplete DNA, so the team combined his genome with a younger tortoise’s DNA, resulting in a code that was only about 95 percent Jonathan—and allowing for the possibility that some of his unique DNA variants were not included in the sample. A blood test would have produced a full genome, but because of the risk of infection for the tortoise, Saint Helena officials did not allow it.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: What’s more, Jonathan is just one study subject, and it’s difficult to generalize any results based on a lone individual. His genome was also compared against only a small handful of other tortoises, as bioinformatics researcher Kousuke Hashimoto of the University of Osaka, Japan, tells New Scientist’s James Woodford, inviting the possibility that the other tortoises also had unique variants that were not identified. Nevertheless, he calls the study “fascinating.”

“The results integrate very well in the wider puzzle of what longevity is,” Björn Schumacher, who studies aging at the University of Cologne in Germany and was not involved in the study, tells the New York Times.

Jonathan was born in the Seychelles, an island nation in the Western Indian Ocean. But as a gift to the governor, he was brought to Saint Helena in 1882, when he was photographed as an adult. Since then, he has been living at Plantation House, the governor’s home, with other giant tortoises.

Hollins took charge of Jonathan’s care in 2009, when the animal was around 180 years old and not in great shape. Among markers of age, such as cataracts and a loss of smell that prevented him from finding his own food, the tortoise suffered from a soft beak that made it hard to graze. The veterinarian hand-fed Jonathan, who recovered and developed a razor-sharp edge to his beak within the next couple of years.
“He is symbolic of resilience, longevity, endurance,” Hollins tells Reuters’ Marta Serafinko, “a persistent presence throughout huge historic events.”

articles.title: I’m Still Convinced the iPod Was the Perfect Gadget
articles.author: Steven Levy

paras.en: I remember the birth of the iPod, 25 years ago this month. I was working at Newsweek. It was October 23, little more than a month after the attacks on the twin towers of the World Trade Center, and everybody was focused on the aftermath. I didn’t go to Cupertino for the launch, where Steve Jobs pulled the gadget from his jeans pocket and boasted that it contained a whole music library. Apple couriers hand-delivered the device to me in New York, and Jobs got on the phone with me. “iPod,” he told me, “will be a landmark product.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: He was right. By 2004, I was writing a cover story called “iPod Nation,” and later I published a book about the iPod called The Perfect Thing.

The death of the iPod wasn’t as memorable. It’s not even clear when it happened. Officially, one might date the time of death as occurring on May 10, 2022, when Apple discontinued the iPod Touch, the last product to use that name. But I never considered the Touch a real iPod; it was simply an iPhone without cellular connectivity. Maybe the appropriate death call might have been July 27, 2017, when Apple killed the Nano—the last traditional iPod with a screen—and the iPod Shuffle, a postage-stamp-sized player that clipped to your shirt. (Apple had quietly discontinued the classic iPod, with a hard drive and click wheel, in 2014.)
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: All these final dates were an inevitable consequence of what Steve Jobs put in motion on January 11, 2007. That’s when he announced three new products—a phone, an internet device, and “the best iPod ever,” all integrated into a new thing called the iPhone. From that moment on, the iPod as a separate device was living on borrowed time.

Still, for years, Apple sold millions more of the beloved devices before the iPod went silent. But even as we love our smartphones, the iPod scratched an itch that still lingers, and I’m sticking to my claim that the iPod was The Perfect Thing. It was a one-function device that superbly executed its function. It made people unconditionally happy. In contrast, our relationships with our iPhones (and Android phones) are more complicated. Yes, the device that superseded the iPod is galaxies more impactful than its predecessor. Financially, of course, it is the engine of a $4 trillion company. I can’t imagine any other contender for the mantle of best product of the century.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But I would not call the iPhone perfect. It gobbles our attention, sometimes with toxic social media apps. Countless cars have been totaled because drivers were more interested in its touch screen than what was happening on the other side of the windshield. iPhone doomscrolling can result in depression. Whereas that perky iPod brought nothing but joy.

Adding to the excitement was Steve Jobs’ willingness to redesign the iPod every year. Apple could have maintained its original iPod for a long spell, but almost immediately the company began a series of significant reinventions. Every cycle yielded an iPod with a different size and shape. With each iteration, the iPod seemed to grow smaller and cooler. First came the mini, then came multiple variations of nanos and shuffles in crazy colors and configurations. iPhone updates have kept people buying, but without the fun of a total reshaping of the product.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Is there an alternate universe where Apple continued making the iPod as a dedicated digital music player? I called Tony Fadell to discuss. Fadell is often referred to as the father of the iPod; he headed its hardware team and delivered the product in an amazing sprint of less than a year. He later was deeply involved in developing the iPhone, and his post-Apple career includes cofounding Nest, becoming a successful tech investor, and writing a well-received book.

Fadell resigned from Apple in 2008 and consulted for two years after that, when Apple was still supporting the iPod. But he recalls Jobs and other execs agreeing that the device was on a course to oblivion, despite being a great product with an enthusiastic user base. With the iPhone proving to be a monster success that also helped boost the Macintosh, and Apple pursuing potentially mass-market innovations like the iPad, iPod sales were becoming less relevant to the company’s bottom line. Jobs was a relentless prioritizer, and his successor Tim Cook felt the same way.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Fadell says that there was very little hand-wringing about the iPod’s fate. “The discussion was about Apple [not] doing lower-value things,” he says. Yet he agrees with me that the iPod’s disappearance created a hole that hasn’t been filled.

In retrospect, he says, what made the iPod invaluable is what it didn’t do—connect with the internet. “Because the iPod wasn't connected, you didn’t have all these other things going on to distract you. Today, you get all the annoyance of being connected without being able to get the same listening experience. You can always be distracted and go somewhere else.”
“This thing should still exist,” he says.

A lot of people seem to agree. There are multiple active communities on Facebook and Reddit of refuseniks who go to great lengths to mod old iPods—putting in large flash drives, installing Bluetooth. There’s even an app that makes your iPhone look and play like an iPod Classic. It works great, but you’re still one swipe away from your feeds, your mail, and everything else in your life that isn’t as fun as music.

I ask Fadell how he regards the iPod’s legacy. Tellingly, his answer speaks to Apple’s history more than exhilaration for the product itself. “The iPhone never would have existed without it,” he says. “That means that the Apple we know of would never have existed without the iPod.” It helped turn a computer company with a limited user base into a consumer electronics giant.
“And the crazy thing is that it was exactly 25 years ago—which is half the years that Apple has existed. There was the Apple II, and then the Mac, and then, boom,” he adds.

I prefer to remember the iPod for what it was, not what it led to. Not long ago, I exhumed my iPod Classic. I have an old boombox with a cradle designed for the iPod, with the old 30-pin connector. I put it in shuffle mode and blissed out.

I suspect a lot of others might like to return to iPod Nation. New CEO John Ternus has no incentive to revive the product, of course. I do find it sad, however, that a generation exists that doesn’t know what it’s like to have a dedicated music device that will never interrupt a tune with calls, texts, and notifications. They don’t know what they’re missing.

articles.title: The DOJ Is Weighing Perjury Charges Against Cassidy Hutchinson
articles.author: Hugo Lowell

paras.en: Federal prosecutors have been weighing a perjury and obstruction-of-justice case against Cassidy Hutchinson, who implicated President Donald Trump in the January 6 Capitol riot in testimony four years ago, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

The efforts mark the Justice Department’s intent to proceed against Hutchinson, a former aide to ex-Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, though prosecutors are not expected to ask a federal grand jury in Washington to return an indictment until at least after the midterm elections, the sources say.

Hutchinson testified as a star witness to the committee that investigated the riot, recounting that Trump encouraged his supporters to march to the Capitol even though he knew many were armed. She sat for several interviews in addition to her public testimony, where she recalled hearing that Trump had lunged at one of his Secret Service agents after being told he could not join his supporters at the Capitol.

In recent months, prosecutors at the Justice Department have focused on the fact that the former special counsel, Jack Smith, did not corroborate much of Hutchinson’s account to the committee, and the Secret Service’s denial of any altercation in the presidential limo, the sources say.

By comparing the transcripts of Hutchinson’s interviews with the committee and against her testimony to Smith’s team, prosecutors have been trying to construct a case based on how her testimony has changed, the sources say.

Prosecutors have also taken a special interest in Hutchinson’s claim that she had penned a statement on a notecard for Trump to release during the Capitol riot—a claim disputed by former Trump White House counsel Eric Herschmann, who said he had written the note.

It was not immediately clear whether prosecutors intend to ultimately proceed with both perjury and obstruction charges, which have been under consideration for several months. The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Hutchinson and her lawyer did not respond to texts and calls seeking comment. Hutchinson, now 29, has kept a low profile since publishing a memoir of her time in Trump’s first administration in 2023 titled Enough.
Punchbowl News first reported the Justice Department’s interest in charging Hutchinson.

The grand jury investigation is the latest example of the Justice Department pursuing criminal cases against Trump’s perceived political enemies. Trump fired former US attorney general Pam Bondi in April partly for moving too slowly to bring such cases, sources familiar with the matter said.

Some Justice officials have been skeptical about whether there is a viable criminal case against Hutchinson, in part due to the high bar for successfully prosecuting perjury charges, the sources say. To prove that Hutchinson lied to Congress, prosecutors would need to show beyond a reasonable doubt that Hutchinson lied, that she did so knowingly, and that it materially impacted the investigation, former US attorney Joyce Vance tells WIRED.

The investigation into Hutchinson became a priority for the DOJ after a criminal referral by Representative Barry Loudermilk, a Georgia Republican who for years has been deeply critical of the January 6 committee investigation. Loudermilk had separately sought to depose Hutchinson until he was blocked by House speaker Mike Johnson, who was concerned it could surface damaging texts of a sexual nature between lawmakers and Hutchinson.

In an unorthodox move, the referral ended up getting assigned to the Civil Rights Division at the DOJ, as opposed to the US Attorney for the District of Columbia or the Criminal Division, which would usually handle public corruption cases.

Under Justice Department guidelines, the Civil Rights Division is only supposed to take cases with a nexus to a civil rights violation. The division is led by Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump loyalist who has been a reliable advocate for the Trump administration's prosecutorial agenda.

articles.title: NASA Just Made Nearly 1 TB of Artemis II Data Available to the Public
articles.author: Jorge Garay

paras.en: NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.

The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.

In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.

Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.

For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.

For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.

Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.

The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.

articles.title: Jets' Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell ruled out for Browns game

paras.en: Oct. 9 (UPI) -- New York Jets running back Breece Hall and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell are ruled out for Week 5's game against the Cleveland Browns, coach Aaron Glenn told reporters Friday.
Glenn also said that left guard Dylan Parham and linebacker Kiko Mauigoa will not play Sunday.

Hall, who sustained a quadriceps injury in Week 3, would miss his second consecutive game. Mitchell missed the last two weeks due to a finger injury. Parham and Mauigoa are out with respective knee and quad injuries.

Second-string running back Braelon Allen started in place of Hall in the Jets' 23-12 loss to the Chicago Bears on Sunday in Chicago. He was in for 30 (94%) of the Jets' offensive snaps and totaled 67 yards from scrimmage off 16 touches. No other Jets running back logged a rushing attempt against the Bears.
Hall, who hasn't practiced since Week 3, totaled 265 yards from scrimmage and a score through his first three appearances this season.

Mitchell caught nine passes for 123 yards through his two appearances this season. The Jets started Garrett Wilson and Isaiah Williams at wide receiver over the last two weeks. Jordan Meredith filled in for Parham at left guard.

Glenn said defensive back Jarvis Brownlee, who is in the concussion protocol, is progressing well. Tight end Mason Taylor, who missed the last two games due to a thumb injury, is set to return in Week 5.
The Jets (1-3) will host the Browns (3-1) at 1 p.m. EDT Sunday in East Rutherford, N.J.

articles.title: Watch: Hundreds of Spider-Man fans attempt world record at NYCC

paras.en: Oct. 9 (UPI) -- Hundreds of Marvel fans donned Spider-Man costumes at New York Comic Con in an attempt to break a Guinness World Record.

The Thursday event, organized by toy company Jazwares in collaboration with Disney Consumer Products, attempted to break the Guinness World Record for the largest gathering of people dressed as Spider-Man.
Organizers have not yet released an official count from the event, but acknowledged the final tally was just short of the current record of 685 participants.
The current record was set by Sony Pictures Entertainment Malaysia in 2023 to celebrate the theatrical release of Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse.

articles.title: Trump forms committee to investigate Fed Gov. Lisa Cook

paras.en: Oct. 9 (UPI) -- President Donald Trump established a committee of inquiry Friday to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook on allegations she made false statements in respect to "one or more mortgage instruments."

He announced the committee in a memorandum posted on the White House website. The committee comprises Kevin Hassett, Trump's adviser on economic policy; Keith Sonderling, labor secretary and acting director of the Office of Government Ethics; and Andrea Lucas, the chairman of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Trump's memo said that it's his job to fire "subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law." He said the committee would investigate and "report to me whether there is 'cause' for Governor Cook's removal."

Trump first attempted to fire Cook from the Federal Reserve in 2025, accusing her of committing mortgage fraud in a loan application by incorrectly listing a property as a vacation home. The Supreme Court ruled against that effort in June, saying Trump needed proper justification.

In August, the Trump administration sent Cook a letter laying out its allegations and seeking a written response within 21 days. She said Trump has "no legal basis" to fire her and said the error on her mortgage loan application was an error.

"An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing," Cook's attorneys said in a statement. "These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will."

articles.title: Executive Turntable: Dasha Smith Named COO of CAA, Warner Music MENA Expands Leadership
articles.author: Ariel King

paras.en: Creative Artists Agency (CAA) has named Dasha Smith the booking agency’s new chief operating officer on Monday (Oct. 5). She joins the agency from the NFL, where she served as executive vp, chief administrative officer.

“Dasha is a remarkably talented, accomplished and energetic leader with a deep understanding of how global organizations operate at their very best,” CAA co-chairman and CEO, Bryan Lourd, said in a statement. “We look forward to welcoming her to our senior management team and benefiting from her significant experience helping to guide leading media and sports organizations.”

Smith added, “I have tremendous respect for the industry leadership position that CAA and its management team continue to build on every year. Even greater is my appreciation for its widely admired, consistent mission to deliver the best possible service and resources to its clients. Joining a culture with that kind of clarity and purpose is an extraordinary opportunity.”
Smith has previously served as executive vp, global chief human resources officer at Sony Music Entertainment and as managing director, office of the chairman at GCM Grosvenor. — Ariel King
Warner Music Middle East & North Africa Expands Leadership

Warner Music Middle East and North Africa (MENA) has expanded its leadership team, with Ahmed Nureni promoted to managing director, MENA, reporting to Guillermo Gonzalez, president of EMEA, recorded music. Ahmad Alghawanmeh joins as general manager, MENA, reporting to Nureni.

“I’m excited to be stepping into this new role at Warner Music MENA,” Nureni said in a statement. “I’m proud of what we’ve achieved in the region over the last few years, but know there is so much more opportunity for growth and development. With Ahmad joining our team, we are now in the best position to capitalize on these opportunities and become the number one destination for artists across the Arab world.”

Alghawanmeh added, “I’m delighted to join Ahmed and the talented teams across the region at such a pivotal moment for Warner Music and the industry. The Arab world has a rich and dynamic creative culture. By combining WMG’s global resources with our local expertise, we’re well positioned to be an empowering home for Arab artists and a strong partner in driving their commercial and creative growth.” — Ariel King
See more music industry hirings and promotions below.

- Michael McCall (Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum) Longtime writer, editor and curator Michael McCall is set to retire from his role as associate director of editorial at the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum at the end of the year, following more than two decades of service to the museum. His final day with the museum will be Dec. 31.

He joined the museum in 2006. In his current role, McCall manages the development of written content for the museum’s exhibitions, books, public programs, website, social media and educational materials. McCall has curated or co-curated over 20 museum exhibits, among them the recent Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker exhibit and past exhibits including Western Edge: The Roots and Reverberations of Los Angeles Country Rock and Family Tradition: The Williams Family Legacy. He also co-edited the second edition of the museum’s Encyclopedia of Country Music, which was published by Oxford University Press. Additionally, McCall has hosted museum programs, interviewing artists and Country Music Hall of Fame members including Brooks & Dunn, Kenny Chesney, Charlie Daniels, Reba McEntire and Wynonna Judd. He also wrote exhibition catalogs on Loretta Lynn and McEntire and authored a book on the museum’s archival collection.

paras.en: “From the beginning of his tenure, Michael’s impressive journalistic sensibilities helped to establish the museum’s editorial voice,” Kyle Young, CEO of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum, said in a statement. “He brings broad historical knowledge with an innate ability to not only understand the music and the people behind it, but also place it within the greater cultural context. Before he joined the museum, he was a talented journalist and well respected by artists and musicians alike. We were lucky to have him and grateful for his two decades of service enlightening and educating us all.”

I will forever appreciate the opportunity given to me by Kyle Young, Liz Thiels and Jay Orr to work alongside a talented, committed staff in continuing the museum’s sanctified mission.”

Prior to joining the museum, McCall served as senior editor for Country Music magazine from 1999 until 2003, and was a regular contributor to the Associated Press, Journal of Country Music, Los Angeles Times, Nashville Scene, Oxford American, People and other publications. From 1984 to 1990, he served as senior music writer for the Nashville Banner. McCall was the recipient of the Charlie Lamb Award for Excellence in Country Music Journalism in 2007. — Jessica Nicholson

- Guy Moot (NMPA) Guy Moot, CEO/chairman of Warner Chappell Music, has been appointed to the National Music Publishers’ Association Board of Directors. Moot says of the appointment that “standing up for songwriters’ rights has never been more critical.” David Israelite, president and CEO of NMPA, adds “The NMPA Board will benefit greatly from his perspective and expertise after over 30 innovative years in the industry,” and that Moot is “one of the most distinguished creative and business minds in music.” — Kristin Robinson

paras.en: - Kate Guarente-Smith (Splice) Splice has named Kate Guarente-Smith the company’s new head of communications. “Kate has a track record of building comms programs that bring diverse audiences into the fold, and helping people see what’s possible for them as technology evolves,” Kakul Srivastava, Splice’s CEO, said in a statement. “I experienced this first-hand during our time together at GitHub. As Splice pushes the edges of what’s possible when AI is used to supercharge human creativity — without flattening in — telling our story with the musicians who trust us to put them first is critical.” Guarente-Smith added, “I’ve always been drawn to companies that believe cutting-edge technology is an enabler and multiplier for human creativity. In many ways, Splice is the truest embodiment of this ethos: music is both deeply personal and a shared cultural touchstone. When technology is introduced in a way that centers the artist and expands the palate of what’s possible, we all win.” — Ariel King

The company also announced a new agreement with AdShare leading the Japanese entertainment company, Pony Canyon. “We’re thrilled to have Sebastian join GoDigital Music and lead our efforts across APAC,” Jason Peterson, founder and chairman, said in a statement. “Sebastian brings a deep understanding of the market and strong relationships across the industry. Our partnership with Pony Canyon is a great place to start, and we see a tremendous opportunity to bring the technology, services and expertise we’ve built at GoDigital Music to more artists, labels and rights holders throughout the region.” Mair added, “GoDigital Music has built a truly global platform, and I’m excited to join the company at a moment when there is so much opportunity across APAC. The region is home to some of the world’s most influential music companies and catalogs, and I look forward to connecting my local expertise with GoDigital Music’s global reach and infrastructure. Our collaboration with Pony Canyon is just the beginning of the kind of work and long-term partnerships we hope to build.” — Ariel King

She was co-owner of Romeo Entertainment Group, where she holds experience in talent buying. “Talent buying and artist representation are very different roles, but they share a common purpose: connecting artists with audiences in meaningful ways,” Romeo said in a statement. “Having spent years working alongside agents to create memorable live experiences, I’m excited to bring a buyer’s perspective to Reliant and help create new opportunities for the artists they represent.” — Ariel King

As he did at War Child UK, Williams will help Children in Conflict deepen its relationship with the music and entertainment communities, working closely with COO Jodi Murphy. As part of the organization’s efforts to tap into the music community, Jim Brenner will lead a newly formed music team at Children in Conflict alongside Dawn Kamerling. Their work will help raise funds for children affected by war by harnessing the ability of artists, the music business and live events. — Chris Eggertsen

paras.en: - Dusty Miller (Big Loud Records) Big Loud Records has named Dusty Miller as president of catalog acquisitions, where he will lead the company’s strategy to source, evaluate and acquire music catalogs and other music-related assets. Miller previously served as founder/president of Miller Wealth Sports & Entertainment, and prior to launching his own firm, he spent 13 years with Truist Bank (formerly SunTrust), serving as an advisor specializing in clients across sports and music.

“This is an exciting day for Big Loud,” Seth England, partner and CEO at Big Loud, said in a statement. “As partners, we have long talked about developing a catalog acquisition component to our business. Dusty has spent many years on the financial side of the music catalog business and has proven to be an expert in his field.”

“I’m incredibly excited to join Big Loud and help build the next chapter of its catalog acquisition business,” Miller added. “I’m especially grateful to Seth, Craig, and Joey for their trust and for the opportunity to be part of such an entrepreneurial and forward-thinking organization. What they’ve built at Big Loud is incredibly special, and I’m excited to be a part of where it goes from here.” — Jessica Nicholson

- Hirings, Promotions at River House Artists River House Artists has announced new hires and promotions across three divisions — publishing, records and management — including promoting two staffers and adding six new staffers. TC Courtney has been named River House’s new director of A&R, and has had prior career stops at Universal Music Publishing Group, Big Machine Label Group and BMI. Alyssa Lawson has joined as manager of digital marketing & artist development, and has prior career stops include MCA and Crowd Surf. Sydney Riley has been promoted to manager, creative services. articles.title: Zara Larsson Receives Award From The Trevor Project: ‘I Want Young People in This Community to Know That I See Them’
articles.author: Paul Grein

paras.en: The Trevor Project, the leading suicide prevention and crisis intervention organization for LGBTQ+ young people, presented Zara Larsson with its 2026 mental health champion of the year award, celebrating her longstanding advocacy for LGBTQ+ people and her openness about mental health.

The annual award spotlights influential public figures who use their voices to challenge stigma, shift culture and advocate for the mental health and well-being of young LGBTQ+ people. Larsson is the sixth recipient of the award, following four other major pop stars — Megan Thee Stallion (2025), Dua Lipa (2024), Janelle Monáe (2022) and Lil Nas X (2021) — as well as social media personality, actress and singer Dylan Mulvaney (2023), who is transgender.

“I’ve never understood the idea of having a platform and not using it to speak up about the things you believe in,” Larsson said in a statement. “LGBTQ+ people have shown me so much love throughout my career, and I want young people in this community to know that I see them, I support them, and they should always feel free to be exactly who they are. I’m incredibly honored to receive this award and proud to stand alongside The Trevor Project in supporting LGBTQ+ young people.”

“Zara Larsson has built a career around the idea that joy, self-expression, and being unapologetically yourself are things worth celebrating,” said Jaymes Black, CEO of The Trevor Project. “She has consistently stood alongside LGBTQ+ people, championed LGBTQ+ voices within her own creative community and used her platform to make clear that everyone deserves the freedom to live openly and authentically. Just as importantly, she has been willing to speak candidly about her own mental health and the importance of asking for and accepting support.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Larsson has publicly spoken out in support of transgender people and trans rights, headlined major Pride celebrations and frequently credited her LGBTQ+ fans for the influence they have had on her music and creativity. She has also used her platform to speak candidly about mental health and help destigmatize conversations around seeking support. She partnered with Maybelline’s Brave Together mental health initiative in 2024.

Larsson, 28, is coming off the biggest year of her career to date. She was a Grammy nominee at the ceremony in February for “Midnight Sun,” which was nominated for best dance pop recording. She received the breakthrough award at Billboard‘s Women in Music event at the Hollywood Palladium in April. “Midnight Sun” reached No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 in September. Also, she reached No. 6 as the featured artist on PinkPantheress’ “Stateside” and No. 35 with her own “Lush Life.”

articles.title: Victrola’s Latest Turntable & Speaker Prove Listening to Vinyl Doesn’t Have to Be Complicated
articles.author: Camila Quimper

paras.en: All products and services featured are independently chosen by editors. However, Billboard may receive a commission on orders placed through its retail links, and the retailer may receive certain auditable data for accounting purposes.
paras.zh: 所有推荐的产品和服务均由编辑独立选择。但是， Billboard可能会收到通过其零售链接下达的订单的佣金，并且零售商可能会收到某些用于会计目的的可审计数据。

paras.en: Building a vinyl collection is one thing. Figuring out how to play those records properly is another. Between choosing the right turntable, finding compatible speakers and navigating a sea of audio terminology, getting into vinyl can feel unnecessarily complicated. And while all-in-one record players offer an easy entry point, their sound quality often leaves something to be desired.
paras.zh: 建立黑胶唱片收藏是一回事。弄清楚如何正确播放这些唱片是另一回事。在选择合适的转盘、寻找兼容的扬声器和浏览大量的音频术语之间，进入黑胶唱片可能会感到不必要的复杂。虽然多合一唱片播放器提供了一个简单的切入点，但其音质往往有待改进。

paras.en: Victrola is looking to bridge that gap with its Wave turntable and Soundstage speaker, a pairing that promises a more substantial listening experience without the elaborate setup. We put both to the test to see how they work together, and while there are a few trade-offs, there’s plenty to like.
paras.zh: Victrola希望通过其Wave转盘和Soundstage扬声器弥合这一差距，这种配对承诺无需精心设置即可获得更丰富的聆听体验。我们对这两者进行了测试，看看它们是如何协同工作的，虽然有一些权衡，但有很多值得一看的地方。

paras.en: The Wave is a manual belt-drive turntable equipped with an Audio-Technica AT-VM95E cartridge, Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity and support for 33 1/3 and 45 RPM records. It also features Auracast technology, which allows audio to be shared with compatible wireless speakers, plus a built-in switchable phono preamp.
paras.zh: Wave是一款手动皮带驱动转盘，配备Audio-Technica AT-VM95E墨盒、蓝牙5.4连接和支持33 1/3和45 RPM记录。它还采用Auracast技术，允许与兼容的无线扬声器共享音频，以及内置的可切换唱机前置放大器。

paras.en: The Soundstage takes a different approach to speaker placement. Designed to sit directly beneath the turntable, it features a front-facing speaker grille, a down-firing woofer that helps minimize vibrations and multiple connection options, including Bluetooth, RCA, optical and USB-C. There’s also an included remote for adjusting volume and switching inputs.
paras.zh: Soundstage采用不同的扬声器放置方法。它专为直接位于转盘下方而设计，配有前置扬声器格栅、有助于最大限度减少振动的低音喇叭和多种连接选项，包括蓝牙、RCA、光纤和USB-C。还有一个用于调节音量和切换输入的随附遥控器。

paras.en: Aesthetically, the pairing is hard to fault. The stacked configuration looks fantastic, although its space-saving design comes with a catch. While it eliminates the horizontal bulk of traditional bookshelf speakers, the combined height is difficult to ignore, especially compared with more compact starter systems.
paras.zh: 从美学上讲，配对很难出错。堆叠的配置看起来很棒，尽管其节省空间的设计附带了一个捕捉器。虽然它消除了传统书架扬声器的水平体积，但组合高度很难忽视，特别是与更紧凑的起动系统相比。

paras.en: Getting everything connected was surprisingly straightforward, with the Wave’s built-in preamp allowing it to work directly with the Soundstage through RCA cables. No complicated wiring or additional audio equipment required.
paras.zh: 让一切连接起来非常简单， Wave内置的前置放大器允许它通过RCA电缆直接与Soundstage一起工作。无需复杂的布线或额外的音频设备。

paras.en: As for the sound? Pretty good, actually. The Soundstage has enough power to fill a room with music, although it doesn’t quite have the depth or stereo separation you’d get from a dedicated pair of bookshelf speakers. It’s a noticeable difference, particularly if you’re used to a more traditional stereo setup.
paras.zh: 那声音呢？其实不错。Soundstage有足够的能量让房间里充满音乐，尽管它没有像专用的一对书架扬声器那样的深度或立体声分离。这是一个明显的区别，特别是如果您习惯了更传统的立体声设置。

paras.en: One thing we kept wishing for was more control over the audio. The included remote handles the basics, but a few additional settings to fine-tune the bass, treble and overall crispness would have made a difference, especially when switching between different records.
paras.zh: 我们一直希望能更好地控制音频。附带的遥控器可以处理基本问题，但一些额外的设置来微调低音、高音和整体脆度会有所不同，尤其是在不同唱片之间切换时。

paras.en: Still, for a speaker designed to make vinyl listening less complicated, there’s a lot to appreciate.
paras.zh: 尽管如此，对于旨在使黑胶唱片聆听变得不那么复杂的扬声器来说，还有很多值得欣赏的地方。

paras.en: Victrola’s Wave and Soundstage feel less like a beginner’s setup and more like a natural next step for someone ready to take vinyl listening a little more seriously.
paras.zh: Victrola的Wave和Soundstage感觉不像是初学者的设置，更像是准备更认真地听黑胶唱片的人的自然下一步。

paras.en: It’s not a replacement for a full hi-fi system, particularly for listeners who prioritize detailed sound customization. But it’s attractive, intuitive and capable of doing exactly what it sets out to do: take the confusion out of building a vinyl setup and put the focus back on the music.
